title: SMT. RANO SINGH . VS. SH. GURBAX SINGH (D) TH LRS

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1137
Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 1 of 51
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7025 OF 2012
SMT. RANO SINGH AND OTHERS ... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SH. GURBAX SINGH (D) TH LRS
AND OTHERS ... RESPONDENT(S)
J U D G M E N T
ARAVIND KUMAR, J.
1. Heard.
2. The instant appeal is filed by the Plaintiffs who are the legal
heirs of late Shri. Sohan Singh, challenging the Judgment and
order of the High Court of Delhi1 passed in RFA No.377/2010
1 Hereinafter referred to as the "High Court"

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 2 of 51
dated 02.02.2012 whereunder the Judgment and decree passed
by Additional District Judge, Tis Hazari, Delhi2 dated
14.01.2010 in Case No. M-27/2009 (old Suit No.475/1975)
dismissing the suit for possession came to be affirmed.
3. For the sake of convenience, the parties herein shall be referred
in terms of their nomenclature, rank and status before the Trial
Court, i.e., Appellants as legal heirs of Sohan Singh or
Plaintiffs and the Respondent No. 1 as Defendant No. 1. As
Respondents No. 2 to 10 are also the legal heirs of Sohan Singh
and they are seeking identical relief to that of the Plaintiffs,
hence, their claims are not discussed separately.
4. Before we proceed to formulate the question of law for
adjudication of facts, we deem it necessary to first set out the
inter se relationship between the parties to the suit and their
respective legal heirs for better understanding. Accordingly,
genealogical chart depicting the relationship between the
parties to this lis and their rank as per the Trial Court and before
this Court is set out hereinbelow -
2 Hereinafter referred to as the "Trial Court"

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 3 of 51
5. The dispute between the parties relate to Plot No.8, Friends
Colony, New Delhi admeasuring approximately 4,132 sq.yds.,
together with the super-structure constructed thereon, which,
for the ease of reference shall be referred to as "plot" or "suit
property" hereinafter.

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 4 of 51
CASE AND ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE
PLAINTIFFS
6. Sohan Singh is the father of Plaintiffs, S. Mukhinder Singh and
S. Sukhinder Singh. He became the member of Nathu Ram
Friends Colony Co-operative Housing Building Society3 Ltd.
on 16.01.1950 and was allotted the suit property by way of an
Agreement to Sell dated 14.01.1952, with an express condition
that he has to raise construction over the plot within a stipulated
time-period of three years. In accordance with the said written
agreement, Sohan Singh paid the sale consideration of Rs.
11,824/- along with other charges.
7. Sohan Singh had close friendly/brotherly relations with Sobha
Singh and they also shared a commercial relationship as
partners in a firm. Thus, Sohan Singh entrusted all matters
relating to the suit property to Sobha Singh, who was acting as
his agent in respect thereof. Since Sohan Singh was at Shimla,
the construction of the house was assigned to Sobha Singh,
who carried out the same. After the completion of the
construction, Sohan Singh wrote a letter to the Society
evidencing the completion of construction and contends that
3 Hereinafter referred to as the "Society"

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 5 of 51
the ownership of Sohan Singh was duly recorded in Resolution
No. 6 dated 30.08.1959.
8. The dispute, according to the Plaintiffs arose when the Society
decided to transfer the plot to Defendant No. 1 vide meeting
held on 13.12.1959, despite duly recording that Sohan Singh is
the owner of the plot. Although the sale consideration was paid
by Sohan Singh, the Society vide Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960
transferred the plot to Defendant No. 1, by way of a sham and
voidable document. The Plaintiffs further contended that the
plot exclusively belonged to Sohan Singh and that, aggrieved
by the execution of the Sale Deed in favour of Defendant No.
1, Sohan Singh approached the Society on 14.05.1963 seeking
execution of the Sale Deed in his favour upon completion of
the construction. However, by letter dated 23.05.1963, the
Society informed him that the plot originally allotted to him
had already been transferred in favour of Defendant No. 1 and
that the Sale Deed had been executed on 03.12.1960.
9. The Plaintiffs, alleging that the Society, in collusion with
Defendant No. 1, fraudulently transferred the plot in favour of
Defendant No. 1, approached the Registrar of Co-operative
Society for redressal of his grievance, through arbitration
proceedings. However, the Society thereafter approached the

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 6 of 51
Registrar of Co-operative Societies, which permitted the
Society to institute a civil suit before the Competent Court. The
Society filed Suit No. 235 of 1966 seeking declaration that the
Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960 executed in favour of Defendant
No. 1 as valid and also sought perpetual injunction against the
Plaintiffs. Subsequently, the Plaintiffs instituted the Suit No.
475 of 1975 (subject suit) seeking of possession of the plot
along with mesne profits. In support of the contentions raised
Appellants have relied upon the following judgments.
i. Poona Ram vs. Moti Ram (Dead) Through Legal
Representatives and Others; (2019) 11 SCC 309.
ii. Narasamma and Others vs. A. Krishnappa (Dead)
Through Legal Representatives; (2020) 15 SCC 218.
iii. Umadevi Nambiar vs. Thamarasseri Roman Catholic
Doicese; (2022) 7 SCC 90.
CASE AND ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE
DEFENDANT NO. 1
10. The Defendant No. 1, Gurbax Singh, son of Sobha Singh,
contended that the suit be dismissed on the following amongst
other contentions -

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 7 of 51
11. Notwithstanding the initial allotment of the plot in favor of
Sohan Singh, the Defendant No. 1 categorically submitted that
Sohan Singh failed to satisfy an essential covenant of the
Agreement, which obligated him to raise construction on the
suit property within a stipulated timeframe. He asserted that
Sohan Singh lacked the financial means to undertake such
construction and, consequently, by way of a letter dated
04.10.1954, requested the Society to transfer the plot to
Defendant No. 1, whom he described therein as his "nephew".
12. Acting upon the letter of Sohan Singh recommending the
transfer of the suit property in favour of Defendant No. 1, the
Society, by resolution dated 13.10.1954, resolved to transfer
the plot to Defendant No. 1. Thereafter, by letter dated
16.10.1954, the Society informed Defendant No. 1 of the
recommendation made by Sohan Singh and directed him to
clear all outstanding dues. Subsequently, by letter dated
22.11.1954, the Society informed Sohan Singh that the plot had
been allotted to Defendant No. 1.
13. Pursuant thereto, Defendant No. 1 took possession of the plot
in 1954, discharged all outstanding dues payable to the Society
entirely and, from his own funds, constructed a two-storeyed
residential house thereon, which was completed by 1959. Since

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 8 of 51
then, Defendant No. 1 has remained in continuous and
uninterrupted possession and occupation of the suit property,
asserting and exercising rights of absolute ownership over the
property. They also denied the contention of the Plaintiffs that
Sobha Singh was acting as an agent of Sohan Singh.
14. In response to the submissions advanced by the Plaintiffs,
Defendant No. 1 contended that Sohan Singh had forfeited all
rights that he previously held in respect of the suit property. On
14.08.1959, Defendant No. 1 informed the Society that the
construction had been completed without any financial
assistance or contribution from Sohan Singh or the Plaintiffs.
15. Alternatively, the Defendant No. 1 also took the contention of
adverse possession on the ground that he has been in
continuous possession of the plot since 1954. In support of their
contentions, they have relied upon following judgments.
i. Ningawwa vs. Byrappa Shiddappa Hireknrabar and
Others; (1968) SCC OnLine SC 206.
ii. Hussain Ahmed Choudhury and Others vs. Habibur
Rahman (Dead) through Lrs. And Others; (2025) SCC
OnLine SC 892.
iii. Anathula Sudhakar vs. P. Buchi Reddy (Dead) by Lrs.
And Others; (2008) 4 SCC 594.

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 9 of 51
iv. Nikhila Divyang Mehta and Another vs. Hitesh P.
Sanghvi and Others; (2025) SCC OnLine SC 779.
v. Prem Singh and Others vs. Birbal and Others; (2006) 5
SCC 353.
vi. Dhurandhar Prasad Singh vs. Jai Prakash University and
Others; (2001) 6 SCC 534.
CASE AND ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY DEFENDANTS
NO. 2 TO 5 (RESPONDENT NOS. 2 TO 10) IN THIS APPEAL
16. The Respondent Nos. 2 to 10 in the present appeal had filed
their written statements before the Trial Court supporting the
plaintiffs and in the present appeal they have reiterated their
stand and sought for the appeal being allowed.
TRIAL COURT AND ITS DECISION
17. Owing to the commonality of issues involved, the suit
instituted by the Society and the suit filed by the Plaintiffs were
consolidated to be tried together and disposed of jointly and the
evidence recorded in the suit preferred by the Society was
ordered to be treated as evidence in the subject suit. However,
the suit of the Society came to be dismissed for default, but the

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 10 of 51
evidence recorded was preserved for the adjudication of the
Plaintiffs suit.
18. The Court initially framed fourteen issues inter alia, question
of limitation, estoppel and on ownership and possession of the
suit property. Further, three additional issues were framed with
regard to the amount involved in construction and payment of
the sale consideration by Sohan Singh. Since we are dealing
with the most significant questions of law, we confine
ourselves to those questions specifically challenged before us.
19. Defendant No. 1 argued that the suit is not maintainable as the
Plaintiffs have sought for possession without seeking any relief
of specific performance or cancellation of the Sale Deed dated
03.12.1960. On evaluation, the Trial Court observed that the
issue of the validity of the Sale Deed was already framed as an
issue and since damages were not claimed by the Plaintiffs, the
only relief left was of possession. Thus, on the said score, Trial
Court admitted the suit.
20. The Trial Court, on the aspect of limitation, held in favour of
the Plaintiffs. It came to be held that dispute arose in 1963
when the Plaintiffs came to know of the alleged sale deed
executed in favour of Defendant No. 1. The Plaintiffs raised
the dissonance before the Society and the matter was referred

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 11 of 51
to Arbitration. The Learned Arbitrator was of the opinion that
issue "involved a complicated question of law and fact" and
relegated the parties to approach the Civil Court for proper
adjudication. As a result, the Society filed Civil Suit No.
235/1966 wherein Sohan Singh and the Defendant No. 1 were
arrayed as parties. Realising that the Society had transferred the
plot to the Defendant No. 1, the Plaintiffs filed Civil Suit No.
475/1975 renumbered as Suit No. M-27 of 2009 seeking
possession. Thus, the Trial Court concluded that for the
purpose of limitation, the facts right from 1963 till the filing of
the suit in 1975 are to be considered as the dispute was raised
before other forums before the suit was finally filed in 1975.
21. Nonetheless, on merits, the Trial Court recognised that the
Plaintiffs were estopped from contending that transfer of the
plot to the Defendant No.1 was without consent. This was for
the reason that firstly, Sohan Singh had never given any letter
to Sobha Singh or to Defendant No. 1 derecognising their rights
over the plot, which resultantly, gave Sobha Singh and
Defendant No.1 permissible possession of the suit property.
Secondly, the Society has transferred the plot to the Defendant
No. 1 on the strength of the letter dated 04.10.1954 by Sohan
Singh and no efforts were made to raise any objection to the

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 12 of 51
possession of the Defendant No. 1 over the property till 1975.
Sohan Singh or anyone claiming through him has not
financially contributed for raising the construction or complied
with the conditions stipulated under the agreement dated
14.01.1952 by which the Suit Schedule property was allotted
to Sohan Singh.
HIGH COURT - THE REGULAR FIRST APPEAL AND ITS
JUDGMENT
22. Before the High Court, the parties made submissions on four
issues as enumerated under the impugned order -
a. Application of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property
Act, 1882 to ascertain whether Sohan Singh had become
the owner of the suit property by virtue of part
performance?
b. Whether the sale deed dated 03.12.1960 executed in
favour of the Defendant No. 1 is on account of fraud and
collusion and its effect thereto?
c. Whether the suit filed by the Plaintiffs is barred by
limitation by the operation of Article 59 of the Limitation
Act, 1963?

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 13 of 51
d. Whether the Defendant No. 1 was the owner of the suit
property by virtue of estoppel or by adverse possession?
23. The first aspect dealt with by the High Court was the argument
raised by the Plaintiffs under Section 53A of the Transfer of
Property Act, to the effect that the buyer, and in the instant
case, Sohan Singh, acquired rights over the suit property
pursuant to an agreement entered into between Sohan Singh
and the Society, upon payment of the agreed sale consideration.
The High Court rejected this argument on the premise that the
written agreement dated 14.01.1952, under which the property
was agreed to be sold to Sohan Singh, contained an express
clause obligating him to raise construction on the said plot
within a specified time. To establish readiness and willingness
under Section 53A, Sohan Singh was required to demonstrate
performance of this condition. Instead, being unable to carry
out the construction, Sohan Singh had addressed a letter dated
04.10.1954 to the Society requesting the transfer of the plot in
favor of Sobha Singh.
24. In furtherance, the Court pointed out another critical
observation - Sohan Singh had voluntarily abjured his rights
under the agreement dated 14.01.1952 vide letter dated

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 14 of 51
04.10.1954. Once a person willingly puts an end to the
performance of continuous obligations set out in the
agreement, he cannot thereafter raise a claim under Section
53A of Transfer of Property Act. Thus, the undisputed factual
position as discerned by the High Court was that there was no
transaction between Sohan Singh and Sobha Singh or with
anybody else for the purpose of construction over the said
plot/suit property.
25. The Original purchaser or allottee from the Society of the suit
property was Sohan Singh. The suit was filed by the legal heirs
of Sohan Singh. The Court noticed that during his life time,
Sohan Singh neither revoked his letter nor questioned the sale
deed. In addition to the above, the Court further noted that there
was an intention to transfer the plot and the membership to the
Defendant No. 1 and this intention overrides the nature of
relationship shared between Sohan Singh and Sobha Singh.
26. Discussing the Rules of the Society, the High Court relied on
the Resolution dated 28.11.1954, passed much prior to the sale
deed dated 03.12.1960, which provided that transfer can take
place not only to a close blood relation but also to a friend of
the member of the society. The Court clarified that Sobha
Singh was a close friend of Sohan Singh, but vide letter dated

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 15 of 51
04.10.1954, Sohan Singh refers to Defendant No. 1 as
"nephew" evidencing their close bond and by operation of the
resolution expanding the transfer to non-blood relatives, the
sale in favour of Sobha Singh was validly executed.
27. On limitation, the High Court held that Plaintiffs and their
predecessor in interest, Sohan Singh, had knowledge of the
Sale Deed since 1960 itself which forms an actual and factual
knowledge. This was corroborated by the admission of
Plaintiff No. 1 who specifically admitted that they came to
know of the fraud of execution of the Sale Deed in the year
1960. In any event, registration of the sale deed constituted
deemed notice under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Ergo, the Plaintiffs are said to have notice of the sale deed once
it was duly registered. As per Article 59 of the Limitation Act,
1963, a suit to cancel or set aside an instrument has to be filed
within three years from the date when the facts entitling the
plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled or set aside becomes
known to him. The High Court therefore was of the view that
even if the limitation is computed from the date as stated by the
Plaintiffs, i.e., 1963, the suit is patently barred by limitation as
the challenge to the sale deed ends in the year 1966 and the suit

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 16 of 51
was filed in the year 1975, without challenge to the sale deed
dated 03.12.1960.
28. On the issue of estoppel and the ownership of the Defendant
No. 1, the reasoning of the High Court was based on the law
laid down under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, which
estops an owner from asserting title after intentionally inducing
another to believe and act upon the representation of
ownership. Applying this principle, the Court observed that
Defendant No. 1 acted as the owner of the suit property as per
the letter dated 04.10.1954 by Sohan Singh to the Society as
the Society transferred the plot and the membership to
Defendant No.1. High Court further observed that no amount
was paid or contributed by the Plaintiffs in lieu of the
construction undertaken by the Defendant No. 1.
29. Based on the said reasonings, the High Court while upholding
the Judgement of the Trial Court dismissed the First Appeal of
the Plaintiffs, prompting them to approach this Court by way
of the present Appeal.
30. We have had the opportunity to go through all the documents
placed on record and have given our anxious consideration to
the rival contentions raised by the Learned Counsels appearing

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 17 of 51
for the parties. In our considered opinion, the following point
would arise for our consideration:
"Whether the Judgment of the High Court, which confirmed
the dismissal of the suit for possession passed by the Trial
Court requires interference?"
ANALYSIS, DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
In Re: On Limitation
31. Undisputed facts -
Date of Agreement to Sell in favour
of the Plaintiff executed by Society
14.01.1952
Time period given to complete
construction and for execution of
Sale Deed (3 years)
14.01.1955
Date of Letter submitted by Sohan
Singh to the Society to transfer the
Suit Schedule property in favour of
Gurbax Singh
04.10.1954
Date of Sale Deed registered &
executed in favour of Defendant
No.1 by the Society
03.12.1960 (construction
was completed in 1959)
Date of institution of the suit 1975

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 18 of 51
32. On the issue of limitation, the High Court and the Trial Court
have taken divergent views, while the Trial Court observed that
the suit is maintainable, the High Court rules that the suit is
barred by limitation. The stand of the parties and the Courts
being completely divergent would compel us to discuss each
of their stands independently.
33. The Plaintiffs advanced arguments to the effect that suit had
been instituted within the prescribed period of limitation. Their
specific case was that the Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960 was
executed by playing fraud, pursuant to which the Plaintiffs
raised claims by letter dated 25.04.1964 against the Society by
raising a dispute before the Registrar of Co-operative Societies
resulting in Arbitral Proceedings. However, upon an
application made by the Society, the Registrar, vide order dated
22.01.1966, directed the Society to institute a civil suit before
the competent Court within a period of six months. Hence, the
Society filed a Civil Suit No. 235/1966 against Sohan Singh
seeking declaration that the sale deed registered in favour of
Gurbax Singh was valid along with a prayer for perpetual
injunction. In the said suit, Gurbax Singh was also impleaded
as a party and he filed the Written statement on 21.08.1971

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 19 of 51
claiming title by virtue of sale deed executed by the Society in
his favour on 03.12.1960. Thereafter, the Plaintiffs filed Civil
Suit No.475/1975 for possession on 22.05.1975. Both Suits
were consolidated and ordered that evidence recorded in Civil
Suit No.235/1966 be treated as evidence in Civil Suit
No.475/1975.
34. Defendant No. 1 contended that Plaintiffs had full knowledge
of execution of the Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960 since the very
year of its execution. As recorded by the High Court, Plaintiff
No. 1 too, in his deposition before the Trial Court categorically
admitted that he became aware of the fraud played upon him in
1960. Hence, 1st Defendant advanced submissions to the effect
that suit filed by the Plaintiffs is barred by limitation, inter alia,
all reliefs that have been sought or could be sought by the
Plaintiffs are hopelessly barred by limitation. It is in this
background Trial Court framed Issue No.7 to the following
effect:
"7. Whether the Suit is within Limitation"
35. Three limbs of arguments were presented by the Defendant
No.1 to non-suit the Plaintiffs on the issue of Limitation -
a. Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963: Although the
Plaintiffs have not sought specific performance,

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 20 of 51
arguendo, even if such a relief were to have been sought,
the suit would be barred by limitation. Under Article 54,
a suit for specific performance must be instituted within
three years from the date fixed for performance or, where
no such date is fixed, from the date when the Plaintiff has
notice of the refusal to perform. In the present case, the
limitation period expired in 1963.
b. Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963: If the Plaintiffs
intended to seek a declaration for cancellation of the Sale
Deed dated 03.12.1960, such a suit ought to have been
instituted within three years from the date of execution of
the Sale Deed, as prescribed under Article 59 of the
Limitation Act. However, it was not done so.
c. Article 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963: The Plaintiffs
have sought the relief of possession which must be
instituted within twelve years from the date of
dispossession. In the present case, the period of limitation
expired in 1972, whereas the suit was instituted only in
1975 and was thus barred by limitation.
We deem it apt and appropriate to extract aforesaid Articles of
Limitation Act, 1963 for analysis of the arguments advanced
on this aspect and same is extracted hereinbelow.

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 21 of 51

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 22 of 51
36. Before we embark upon our discussion and reasoning, we
deem it appropriate to analyse the law on limitation application
to the instant case.
37. The law of limitation, as a procedural law, finds its roots in the
maxims "interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium" which means
that it is in the interest of the State that there should be a limit
to litigation and "vigilantibus non dormientibus jura
subveniunt" - the law assists the vigilant and not those who
sleep over their rights. It specifies that a litigant ought to be
diligent, careful and proactive in enforcing and protecting his
rights for a purpose that the litigation ought to be raised before
the cause expires and also to prevent the litigation from being
dragged for a prolonged period of time. It cannot be construed
that the period of limitation bars the court from enforcing
substantive justice. As the scope of the Act specifies, it is to
make sure that the parties knock the doors of the court within
a time bound manner so as to not render their cause otiose. A
substantial cause seeking justice has a lifespan and once the
cause dies, it cannot be revived by dilatory tactics by clinging
to another cause. Thus, the period of limitation cannot be
extended by any party to make it naturally convenient to bring
the cause within the period of limitation.

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 23 of 51
38. In State of Kerala and Others v. V.R. Kalliyanikutty and
Another4
, referring to Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th Edn.,
this Court has supported the existence of statutes of limitation
holding that a dormant claim can be more cruel than bring
justice; the Defendant might not have or would have lost the
requisite evidence needed to prove the case; and a good cause
should be perused with reasonable diligence. What needs to be
seen is that an existing cause is redressed and not the
resurrection of a stale one. Keeping these legal principles in
mind, we shall now advance to the adjudication of the rival
claims. We clarify that the suit filed by the Plaintiffs is one for
possession. However, we also deem it appropriate to discuss
other points for the specific contentions raised by the
Defendant No. 1 and to lay to rest all contentions in that regard.
39. The claim of the Plaintiffs being barred under Article 54 of the
Limitation Act, 1963 -
a. Article 54 primarily provides the limitation period to file
a suit for specific performance. The Plaintiffs, in the
present matter have not sought for specific performance,
but even assuming they had, the suit would be barred by
limitation. As per the Article, a suit for specific
4
(1999) 3 SCC 657

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 24 of 51
performance has to be filed within a period of three years
from the "date fixed for performance or if no such date is
fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that the performance
is refused". For clear understanding we refer to the case
of Ahmadsahab Abdul Mulla (2) Dead by proposed LRs
v. Bibijan & Others5
, which clarified that, when there is a
date for performance of the contract, there is a definite
date for doing that particular act. The second date runs
from the time the plaintiff notices the refusal. Thus, both
dates are definitive and refers to a date from the calendar.
b. First instance - date fixed for performance: The
Agreement to Sell dated 14.01.1952 stipulated a period of
three years within which Sohan Singh was required to
raise construction on the plot. Accordingly, the date fixed
for performance fell due on 14.01.1955. Under Article 54
of the Limitation Act, the period of limitation would
commence from the date so fixed and expire three years
thereafter, i.e., on 14.01.1958. Any suit for specific
performance instituted thereafter would be barred by
limitation.
5
(2009) 5 SCC 462

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 25 of 51
c. Second instance - date of notice of refusal: The period of
limitation would begin from the date on which the
Plaintiffs had notice of refusal to perform. The execution
of the Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960, at the very least,
constituted such refusal. The Plaintiffs contended before
the High Court that they came to know of the Sale Deed
only on 14.05.1963, when they approached the Society for
execution of a Sale Deed in their favour. The Society, vide
letter dated 23.05.1963, informed Sohan Singh that a Sale
Deed had already been executed in favour of Defendant
No. 1. Even reckoning limitation from the date of such
knowledge, the period of three years would have expired
in 1966. The present suit, having been instituted only in
1975, is ex facie barred by limitation.
40. The claim of the Plaintiffs being barred under Article 59 of the
Limitation Act-a. Article 59 of the Limitation Act applies to all suits seeking
to cancel or set aside an instrument or decree, or to rescind
a contract. For present purposes, we are concerned with
the cancellation or setting aside of an instrument. An
instrument is a written document, which may include a
contract, agreement or deed, etc., which is not void ab

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 26 of 51
initio. The limitation under this Article begins three years
from "when the fact entitling the plaintiff to have the
instrument or decree cancelled or set aside or the contract
rescinded first become known to him".
b. A suit for cancellation of a Sale Deed is to be filed within
3 years from the date of sale or from when the party comes
to know of it. Accordingly, a suit seeking cancellation or
setting aside of the Sale Deed dated 03.12.1960 ought to
have been instituted by Sohan Singh within three years
from the date on which the Plaintiffs acquired knowledge
of the facts entitling them to seek such relief. Even
assuming that the Plaintiffs acquired knowledge of the
Sale Deed only on 23.05.1963, when the Society informed
them that the Sale Deed had already been executed in
favour of Defendant No. 1, the period of limitation would
expire in 1966. On the other hand, if limitation is
calculated from the date of execution of the Sale Deed, the
period would have expired in 1963. In either event, the
suit was instituted only in 1975 and was barred by
limitation.
41. The claim of the Plaintiff being barred under Section 27 read
with Article 64 of the Limitation Act -

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 27 of 51
a. Section 27 of the Limitation Act provides for
extinguishment of the right on the lapse of the period of
limitation fixed to institute a suit for possession of any
property. In essence, the right of a person to institute a suit
extinguishes if it is not brought within the prescribed time
period. The right to sue that accrues in a person has to be
enforced within the time prescribed under law.
b. When possession is the moot question, Article 64 also
comes into play. Possession is not based on title and
anyone who claims lawful possession can invoke this
Article within twelve years from the date of
dispossession. It is founded on the principle of prior
possession and subsequent dispossession. The possession
of the Plaintiff can be of any form and dispossession for
the purpose of this Article means taking possession
without the consent of the person who was already in
lawful possession. It involves some active element in the
mind of the person dispossessing a person against his will
with the intention of taking absolute and exclusive control
over the property.
c. Absence of Dispossession - To maintain a suit under
Article 64, the Plaintiffs were required to prove previous

Civil Appeal No. 7025 of 2012 Page 28 of 51
possession which was demonstrated by the Agreement to
Sell under which handed over possession of the plot to
Sohan Singh to raise construction. The second covenant
of dispossession is not established by the Plaintiffs.
Pertinently, Sohan Singh was not dispossessed by any act

Sale does not itself, create any interest or charge on such
